Replication study

Enhanced Triangle Algorithm for Large-Scale SVM

Gupta, M. & Kalantari, B. — An Enhanced Triangle Algorithm for Large-Scale Support Vector Machine Optimization: A Comparative Study with Classical and Modern Solvers. JIDMIS Vol. 3, Issue 9s (2026)

Independent Python/NumPy re-implementation · full protocol (d = 3 – 10,000, n = 5,000 per set, ε = 10⁻³), 3 trials per configuration · September 2026

Replicated

ETA matches SMO's solution quality — distances agree within tolerance at all ten dimensions (4×10⁻⁵ relative at d = 10,000), with sparser support sets.

Replicated

ETA outpaces SMO increasingly with dimension — 3.7× at d = 10,000 against a comparable uncached SMO (paper: 4.6×).

Replicated

ETA accelerates as the hulls separate (326 → 149 iterations over the k-sweep) while SMO's runtime stays flat — the paper's exact signature.

What was implemented

The Triangle Algorithm treats hard-margin SVM as a geometry problem on the convex hulls K, K′ of the two classes. An iterate pair (p, p′) moves by pivots: v ∈ V is a pivot for p when d(p, v) ≥ d(p′, v); if neither class has a pivot, (p, p′) is a witness pair whose perpendicular bisector separates the hulls. TA I decides intersection vs. separation; TA II computes the hull distance by closing the gap between the upper bound d(p, p′) and a lower bound from parallel supporting hyperplanes orthogonal to h = p − p′.

All four of the paper's enhancements are implemented and switchable: joint closest-point updates of the segments [p, v] and [p′, v′]; incremental dot-product caching (O(nd) → O(n) per iteration for revisited pivots); an anti-zig-zag midpoint pivot; and prioritized search over previously used points. The baseline is a hard-margin SMO (maximal-violating-pair selection, C = ∞) in two variants: with an LRU kernel-row cache, and uncached — the cost profile of the original MATLAB baseline.

Correctness was verified against exact QP ground truth (SLSQP over the two probability simplices): ETA and SMO both agree with the QP distance to 10⁻⁵–10⁻¹³ relative error on small instances, and an ablation confirms every enhancement configuration reaches the same distance — in 36 iterations with all enhancements on vs. 327 with all off.

Extension: beyond the midpoint strategy

Since TA II's toward-steps are Frank-Wolfe/Gilbert-type updates, the FW literature offers stronger zig-zag remedies than the paper's midpoint pivot. Two are now implemented as zigzag_strategy options, reusing the weight bookkeeping the algorithm already maintains: away steps (shrink the worst active vertex's weight, Guélat–Marcotte) and pairwise steps (transfer weight from the worst active vertex to the best pivot — the MDM update). Solved to ε = 10⁻⁾:

Iterations / time by anti-zig-zag strategy (src/zigzag_bench.py)
instancenonemidpoint (paper)awaypairwise
Gaussian d=30, n=200158,941 / 6.6 s148,996 / 6.5 s106 / 0.005 s181 / 0.008 s
Gaussian d=100, n=1,000300,000 (maxiter)300,000 (maxiter)15,886 / 0.90 s3,921 / 0.22 s

At tight tolerance the midpoint remedy is nearly ineffective — oscillation re-forms on the new face — while weight-transfer steps cut iterations by two to three orders of magnitude and land closer to the optimum, consistent with the linear convergence of away-step and pairwise Frank-Wolfe over polytopes. At the paper's working tolerance of 10⁻³ the gain is a modest ~11%, which explains why the midpoint heuristic sufficed in the original study. Notably, the paper's own joint closest-point update already solves the classic pathological case (optimum interior to an edge) in a handful of iterations — it is itself a strong anti-zig-zag device.

Extension: optimized ETA vs standard solvers

The paper's future-work section asks for comparisons with up-to-date solvers. The optimized ETA (pairwise strategy) was run against LIBSVM (sklearn SVC, linear kernel), LIBLINEAR (LinearSVC, hinge loss, tuned to recover the geometric margin), our SMO, and a stochastic-subgradient baseline, on the Table-3 protocol; accuracy is each solver's margin 2/‖w‖ against ETA's certified ε = 10⁻⁾ reference interval.

LIBLINEAR is speed-competitive at scale but its margin accuracy degrades past the tolerance at d = 10,000, and it recovers the geometric margin at all only under careful settings (hinge loss, moderate C — squared hinge or very large C misestimate it by 30%+). The subgradient baseline finds a valid separator but never the maximal margin (relative error ≈ 1 at every setting tried). On this synthetic protocol the paper's thesis holds against modern baselines, not just the original MATLAB SMO.

Extension: soft-margin (L2) SVM

The Triangle Algorithm extends exactly to the L2 soft-margin SVM through the classical reduction: min ½‖w‖² + (C/2)Σξᵢ² is a hard-margin problem in the augmented space x̃ᵢ = [xᵢ; eᵢ/√C], whose Gram matrix is K + I/C and whose hulls never intersect. The augmentation is never materialised — the extra coordinates are exactly the convex weights the algorithm already tracks, so every augmented dot product is a cached product plus a sparse diagonal correction. Validated against the exact QP on the explicit augmentation to ~10⁻¹⁰, with a monotone regularisation path.

Soft margins change the geometry: the support is dense (1,000+ support vectors), and toward-steps stall — oscillation spreads across many vertices, so cycle detection rarely fires. The pairwise machinery from the zig-zag extension becomes the algorithm: step_mode='mdm' makes weight transfer the primary step. On overlapping Gaussian classes (means 4σ apart, n = 5,000/set), all solvers targeting the same objective:

Wherever both converge, ETA-mdm and LIBLINEAR agree on the primal objective to six significant figures and on held-out accuracy to 3–4 decimals — the solutions coincide. The high-dimensional, nearly-separable regime is where the geometric approach's advantage lives, for soft margins just as for hard ones; genuinely overlapping data at large C is hard for every dual method as the problem approaches the infeasible hard margin.

Extension: L1 soft margin via reduced hulls

The L1/ν-SVM is the nearest-point problem between reduced convex hulls (Bennett–Bredensteiner; Crisp–Burges): R(V, μ) caps each point's weight at μ = 2/(νl), shrinking the hull toward its centroid — slack as geometry. Two changes adapt the Triangle Algorithm: the extreme point becomes a capped top-k blend (partial sort, still O(n)), and the primary step is the capped MDM transfer, clipped to the box. Validated against the box-constrained QP to 10⁻⁹ and against sklearn's NuSVC (LIBSVM) to ~10⁻¹⁰ via δ = ‖w‖/S with S the per-class dual-coefficient sum. Points at the cap are exactly the margin violators.

Extension: kernelized Triangle Algorithm

The ETA touches data only through inner products, so kernelization changes plumbing, not algorithm: Gram columns become kernel columns, norms become kernel diagonals, and the iterates exist purely as convex weights — no explicit feature vector. Linear, RBF and polynomial kernels are supported, each optionally with a ridge K + I/C for the kernelized L2 soft margin. Validation: the linear kernel reproduces the euclidean ETA to machine precision; RBF distances match the exact kernel QP to ~10⁻⁹, sklearn SVC's hard-margin RBF solution to ~10⁻⁵, and the kernel SMO to ~10⁻⁸.

Extension: real benchmark datasets

Real standards bundled in PyPI packages (the sandbox blocks the usual dataset hosts): UCI Breast Cancer Wisconsin, UCI digits (odd-vs-even and 3-vs-8), and a bundled 5,000-sample MNIST subset (odd-vs-even and 3-vs-8); 75/25 stratified splits, standardized features. TA I first decides hard-margin feasibility for free: wdbc and both 3-vs-8 tasks are linearly separable (high-d, small-n), digits odd-vs-even is certifiably not.

The ν-SVM (reduced hulls vs NuSVC) agrees on distances to 10⁻⁵ with accuracies within a point on every dataset, and the kernelized RBF solver matches KernelSMO to 10⁻⁵ with accuracies within ~1% of the SVC reference — digits odd-vs-even jumps from 0.896 linear to 0.973 kernelized, the expected benefit on a real nonlinear task. The certified duality gap and the feasibility test are capabilities the baselines do not offer.

Extension: gap-certified safe shrinking

shrink=True adds exact safe screening to the distance solver (inherited by the soft-margin and kernel variants). Strong convexity of ½‖x‖² over the Minkowski difference bounds ‖h − h*‖ ≤ r = √(UB² − LB²), so a zero-weight point with (h·vᵢ − h·vmin) > r‖vᵢ − vmin‖ is certifiably outside the optimal support and is removed. The optimum's support provably survives, so the reduced problem has the same optimum and every later certificate stays valid — one O(n) pass per screening round from already-cached quantities.

Validation: shrunk and unshrunk runs agree with the exact QP to 10⁻⁸–10⁻¹¹ across all solver variants, and on small instances screening collapses each class to exactly the QP's optimal support without ever discarding a true support point. On a Table-3-style instance (d = 1000, n = 5000/set) the point set shrinks to 82+93 survivors for a 1.6× wall-clock gain at identical distances. The honest counterpart: on the dense-overlap MNIST soft-margin problem the certificate excludes nothing — the gap never tightens enough for r to bite. Safe screening pays off exactly where the gap closes; dense ill-conditioned problems would need LIBSVM-style heuristic shrinking with reactivation.

Extension: block transfers

step_mode='block' amortises the O(n) scan over up to k weight transfers per iteration: the top-k receivers pair with the worst-k active donors, per-pair magnitudes clip to donor capacity, and one exact line search runs along the aggregated direction — descent guaranteed, single-MDM fallback intact, cache updates batched into single GEMV calls. Block agrees with the exact QP to ~10⁻⁹ and with MDM to ~10⁻¹¹ across all solver variants.

Iteration counts drop 4–30× everywhere and wall-clock improves 1.4–2× on the dense-support problems, with the best block size growing with dimension. On MNIST odd-vs-even the qualitative result matters most: block mode is the only configuration that reaches the certified solution at all — MDM exhausts 200k iterations short of it. Remaining per-iteration overhead is Python-level; a compiled inner loop would multiply these gains.

Convergence theory for the block step

The block step now carries a proof (docs/block_convergence.md). With pair 1 always the MDM/pairwise-FW pair, elementary arguments (triangle inequality + Cauchy–Schwarz) give the gain bound ΔB ≥ ΔMDM/(2k) for the aggregate line-search step under capacity clipping. A guarded variant — take the single MDM step whenever its O(1)-computable gain exceeds the block's, now implemented — makes every iteration's progress at least pairwise FW's, so the guarded algorithm inherits the Lacoste-Julien–Jaggi linear rate with identical constants while doing up to k transfers per scan; unguarded, the rate degrades by at most the explicit factor 2k. A near-orthogonality proposition shows the best case: ΔB approaches the sum of all k pair gains, matching the measured 4–30× iteration reductions and their growth with dimension. Every inequality is verified numerically across 4,000 random ensembles (worst slack at machine precision), 500 near-orthogonal ensembles, and 5,209 instrumented live block steps — none increased the objective.

Consolidated performance

Every problem class in this study, three ways: the paper-style ETA (or plain MDM where toward-steps do not apply), the optimised ETA (block transfers + safe shrinking + MDM as appropriate), and the strongest standard solver per class. Distances agree within tolerance on every row.

Assumptions and caveats

The source study leaves the sampling law, trial count, and k-grid unspecified, so those were reconstructed: uniform-in-unit-ball clouds for the intersection regime, Gaussian clouds (which reproduce the reported distance scales) with k = 1.2 for the dimension sweep and k ∈ [1.2, 1.9] for the sensitivity sweep — the latter lands on distances 54.7–89.8 against the paper's 45.5–78.4. One finding worth noting: the size of the speedup depends on SMO implementation quality. An LRU kernel-row cache alone shrinks TA's edge from 3.7× to 1.5× at d = 10,000 — which supports the paper's own recommendation to extend comparisons to modern solvers such as LIBSVM and ThunderSVM.
